cards.title: Dimension-independent ε⁻³ oracle complexity for smooth online optimization
cards.formal: Is there a projection-free randomized online algorithm whose total number of gradient and linear-optimization oracle calls needed to guarantee expected average regret at most ε is O(ε⁻³), uniformly over the ambient dimension and all compact convex decision sets? More precisely, for every fixed positive D,G,β, seek a bound C(D,G,β)ε⁻³, with C independent of d, the set K and the adversary, for every d≥1, every nonempty compact convex K⊆Rᵈ contained in the radius-D Euclidean ball, every 0<ε<1, and every adaptive sequence of convex β-smooth losses with gradient norm at most G. The algorithm’s guarantee must use only gradient access to revealed losses and linear optimization over K as described below. This is the source’s online average-regret question, not minimization of one fixed smooth function.
cards.why: Would show whether the smoother-loss improvement in online learning can retain its oracle advantage in arbitrarily high dimension and over arbitrary feasible geometry.
cards.status_note: Read the original adaptive game, oracle definitions, theorem statements and Section 6 complexity question. Checked the 2023 LOO comparison, 2024 separation-oracle model, and 2026 adversarial-constraint result; broader searches included stochastic, decentralized and matrix variants. progress.text: The source obtains smooth-loss total oracle complexity O(dε⁻³) and asks to remove d.

cards.definitions: At round t the learner chooses xₜ∈K while the adversary chooses fₜ:K→R. The adversary may depend on the full previous history but cannot observe the learner’s fresh random choice at that round before fixing fₜ. Afterwards the loss is revealed and may be accessed through exact gradient evaluations at queried points of K; future losses are unavailable. Each fₜ is differentiable and convex, ‖∇fₜ(x)‖₂≤G, and ‖∇fₜ(x)−∇fₜ(y)‖₂≤β‖x−y‖₂ for all x,y∈K. After H rounds, regret is R_H=Σ_{t=1}^H fₜ(xₜ)−min_{x∈K}Σ_{t=1}^H fₜ(x). Expectation is over the learner’s randomness and any adversary randomness, including the resulting adaptive history; the required guarantee is E[R_H]/H≤ε. The algorithm may choose its horizon and parameters using ε,D,G,β and d, but its total oracle-call bound must hold uniformly in d and K. A linear-optimization call at v∈Rᵈ returns any maximizer of ⟨v,x⟩ over K; the support value is then obtained by an inner product. All returned points must be valid maximizers, and no special tie-breaking promise is available. Access to K is through this oracle and a feasible starting point, which can also be obtained by a zero-objective call. Every gradient evaluation and every linear-optimization invocation counts once, including initialization, internal repeated calls and calls on past losses. Projection, membership and separation are not additional free oracles. Internal vector arithmetic is not the resource being bounded; this is an exact real-oracle complexity question, not a dimension-independent bit-running-time claim. The displayed O bound hides neither dimension nor geometric conditioning of K, and does not hide logarithmic losses in ε. The target concerns total calls, without requiring exactly one call per online round.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform online algorithm with a total-call bound C(D,G,β)ε⁻³ and expected average regret at most ε for every specified instance and adaptive adversary, or prove that such a uniform bound is impossible in this oracle model. A negative answer must rule out the uniform ε⁻³ bound, rather than merely exhibit a dimension factor in one existing analysis. An algorithm needing extra set geometry, a different free oracle, stronger loss assumptions or more total calls does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: The combined oracle count is the stated resource
context_blocks.text: Section 6 counts both gradient computations and linear optimizations until average regret reaches ε. A regret rate alone is insufficient if achieving it requires many internal oracle calls. The source gives O(dε⁻³) for smooth losses and contrasts it with the previous ε⁻⁴ dependence.

context_blocks.title: Smooth losses and arbitrary sets are both part of the question
context_blocks.text: The source allows arbitrary compact convex feasible sets and an adaptive adversary. Fast results for a special polytope, a curved set, a fixed stochastic objective or strongly convex losses address different restrictions.

context_blocks.title: An improvement under extra assumptions
context_blocks.text: Garber and Kretzu obtain improved bounds for smooth exp-concave losses, with benefits when gradients approximately span a low-dimensional space. Exp-concavity and low-dimensional gradients are not assumptions of this card.

context_blocks.title: A different oracle changes the comparison
context_blocks.text: Mhammedi’s 2024 preprint gives guarantees using a separation oracle, with dimension and geometric parameters in the bounds. It does not supply the specified bound using only linear-optimization access to the set.

context_blocks.title: A newer constrained variant
context_blocks.text: The AISTATS 2026 adversarial-constraint paper uses linear optimization but has a T^{3/4} scale for general losses and an additional constraint-violation objective. Its stated result does not supply the uniform ε⁻³ guarantee here.

cards.context:
Section 6 counts both gradient computations and linear optimizations until average regret reaches ε. A regret rate alone is insufficient if achieving it requires many internal oracle calls. The source gives O(dε⁻³) for smooth losses and contrasts it with the previous ε⁻⁴ dependence.

The source allows arbitrary compact convex feasible sets and an adaptive adversary. Fast results for a special polytope, a curved set, a fixed stochastic objective or strongly convex losses address different restrictions.

Garber and Kretzu obtain improved bounds for smooth exp-concave losses, with benefits when gradients approximately span a low-dimensional space. Exp-concavity and low-dimensional gradients are not assumptions of this card.

Mhammedi’s 2024 preprint gives guarantees using a separation oracle, with dimension and geometric parameters in the bounds. It does not supply the specified bound using only linear-optimization access to the set.

The AISTATS 2026 adversarial-constraint paper uses linear optimization but has a T^{3/4} scale for general losses and an additional constraint-violation objective. Its stated result does not supply the uniform ε⁻³ guarantee here.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
